section.title: Clean and Unclean
section.sectionRationale: Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem confront Jesus over the tradition of the elders. He turns the charge around: their tradition actually nullifies the command of God. Then He redraws the whole map of purity, teaching that defilement is not a matter of hands and food but of the heart.
section.thesis: True defilement comes not from what enters a person from outside but from the sinful heart within, and human tradition that overrides God's word is a hollow, hypocritical worship that Jesus exposes and sweeps away.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the challenge over tradition and Jesus' counter-charge; the public saying about what truly defiles; and the private explanation that traces defilement to the heart.

units.label: The tradition of the elders
units.note: the word of God nullified by tradition

verses.text: Then some Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem and asked,
“Why do Your disciples break the {{paradosis|tradition}} of the elders? They do not wash their hands before they eat.”
Jesus replied, “And why do you break the command of God for the sake of your tradition?
For God said, ‘Honor your father and mother’ and ‘Anyone who curses his father or mother must be put to death.’
But you say that if anyone says to his father or mother, ‘Whatever you would have received from me is a gift devoted to God,’
he need not honor his father or mother with it. Thus you nullify the word of God for the sake of your tradition.
You {{hypokrites|hypocrites}}! Isaiah prophesied correctly about you:
‘These people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me.
They worship Me in vain; they teach as doctrine the precepts of men.’”
Jesus called the crowd to Him and said, “Listen and understand.
A man is not {{koinoo|defiled}} by what enters his mouth, but by what comes out of it.”
Then the disciples came to Him and said, “Are You aware that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this?”
But Jesus replied, “Every plant that My heavenly Father has not planted will be pulled up by its roots.
Disregard them! They are blind guides. If a blind man leads a blind man, both will fall into a pit.”

units.label: It is the heart that defiles
units.note: out of the heart come evil things

verses.text: Peter said to Him, “Explain this parable to us.”
“Do you still not understand?” Jesus asked.
“Do you not yet realize that whatever enters the mouth goes into the stomach and then is eliminated?
But the things that come out of the mouth come from the {{kardia|heart}}, and these things defile a man.
For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false testimony, and slander.
These are what defile a man, but eating with unwashed hands does not defile him.”

paradosis.gloss: That which is handed down, a tradition. Here it is the oral tradition of the elders, the rulings added around the Law. Jesus does not condemn all handing down of truth, but exposes tradition that is raised above and against the written command of God.

hypokrites.gloss: An actor who speaks behind a mask, a pretender. Jesus names the leaders hypocrites because their worship is a performance of the lips while the heart is far from God, the very charge Isaiah leveled.

koinoo.gloss: To make common or unclean, to defile. The ceremonial law spoke of foods and contact that made one unclean; Jesus relocates true defilement from the outside of a person to the heart within, from ritual to moral.

kardia.gloss: The heart, the inner core of a person, the seat of thoughts, desires, and will. In Jesus' teaching the heart, not the hands or the stomach, is the source of what truly defiles, so cleansing must reach that deep.

basic.context: Religious leaders travel from Jerusalem to challenge Jesus: His disciples ignore the tradition of hand washing before meals. Jesus answers with a sharper question. Their traditions actually let people dodge God's own command to honor father and mother. He calls them hypocrites and quotes Isaiah. Then He tells the crowd that a person is not defiled by what goes into the mouth but by what comes out, and privately explains that evil comes from the heart.
basic.hermeneutics: The debate is not about hygiene but about authority: does human tradition or God's word rule? Notice the difference between the ceremonial food laws, which Jesus is beginning to fulfill and set aside, and the moral law of the heart, which stands. The key question is where uncleanness really comes from, and Jesus answers plainly: from within.
basic.originalLanguages: The leaders defend the paradosis, the tradition handed down. Jesus calls them hypokritai, actors wearing a mask, whose lips honor God while the heart is far away. He says nothing entering the mouth can koinoo, defile, a person; defilement rises from the kardia, the heart, the inner spring of thoughts and deeds.
basic.typology: The prophets longed for a day when God would deal with the heart, not just the surface. Jesus, by locating sin in the heart, points ahead to the new covenant promise of a new heart and a cleansing that ritual washing could never give.
basic.christ: Jesus speaks with an authority above the elders and even reframes the purity laws, showing Himself Lord of the Law. He is the one who diagnoses the true disease, the sinful heart, and who alone can cleanse it, making the unclean clean from the inside out.
basic.god: God is not fooled by outward religion. He sees the heart and is grieved by worship that is all lips and no love. He gave commands like honoring parents that tradition must never cancel, and He cares far more about mercy and truth than about ceremonial detail.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 29:13 lies behind these people honor Me with their lips. Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36 promise a new heart. Mark 7 tells the same account and adds that Jesus thus declared all foods clean. Titus 1 speaks of the pure in heart.
basic.oneStory: Jesus exposes a religion of the surface and relocates the real problem to the heart. This sets the stage for the gospel: no washing of hands can cleanse a defiled heart, so the Son of God comes to give His people a new heart and to make the unclean clean by His own blood.

context.literary:
The passage is built as a descending funnel of audiences. First comes the hostile delegation from Jerusalem, then the crowd, then the disciples, and finally Peter alone, who asks the question the others are thinking. Jesus speaks to each at a different depth. To the leaders He gives a charge, to the crowd a riddle, and to the twelve the interpretation. Matthew calls the saying of verse 11 a 'parable', verse 15, which fits his habit in chapter 13 of giving a public word and then a private key.

The opening exchange is a matched pair of questions. The leaders ask why the disciples 'break' the tradition of the elders, verse 2. Jesus throws the same verb back: why do you 'break' the command of God, verse 3. The whole argument turns on that mirror. What they treat as transgression is a breach of human custom; what He names as transgression is a breach of God's word.

Isaiah's oracle, verses 8 and 9, forms the hinge. It names the problem as a split between mouth and heart, and the rest of the chapter works out the heart half. Verse 11 states it as a contrast, 'enters' against 'comes out', and verses 17 to 19 trace the movement from mouth to stomach to drain on one side and from heart to mouth on the other. The vice list at the end ends with slander, the sin of the mouth, and so closes the circle.

Within Matthew the chapter belongs to a run of escalating opposition that began in chapter 12 and continues until the leaders at last seek to destroy Him. It also sets up the next scene: the same Jesus who has just redrawn the line between clean and unclean walks into Gentile territory.
context.historical:
The delegation comes 'from Jerusalem', verse 1, which signals an official inspection rather than a chance encounter. Galilee was a long way from the temple authorities, and a teacher drawing large crowds there would draw their scrutiny.

The 'tradition of the elders' was the body of interpretation and practice the Pharisees had built around the written Torah, meant to put a fence of care around it. Much of it was later gathered in the Mishnah, which has a whole tractate devoted to the washing of hands. The Torah itself asks hand washing of the priests before they minister, Exodus 30:19 to 21, but gives no such rule for ordinary people at an ordinary meal. The Pharisees were seeking to extend priestly purity to every Israelite table, a sincere aim. Behind that lay a conviction that the whole nation was called to holiness, Leviticus 11:44, and the Pharisees wanted to give that calling a daily shape.

The example Jesus chooses is pointed. A person could declare property 'a gift devoted to God', verse 5, and, on the reading Jesus attacks, thereby escape the duty of supporting aged parents with it. Mark, writing for readers less at home in Jewish custom, preserves the Aramaic word Corban for such a gift, Mark 7:11. In a world with no pensions, a parent's old age depended on the children, so the fifth commandment, Exodus 20:12, was a matter of food and shelter. A vow that outranked it turned piety into a loophole.

The food laws were for most Jews the plainest boundary between Israel and the nations. When Jesus says nothing entering the mouth defiles, He touches that boundary directly, which is why the disciples report that the Pharisees were 'offended', verse 12.
context.canonical:
Isaiah 29:13 is the anchor. In its own setting the prophet addressed Jerusalem under Hezekiah, a city full of ritual and short of trust, and the following verses expose people who think they can hide their plans from God, Isaiah 29:15. Jesus applies the same word to a later generation of religious leaders, and Matthew says Isaiah 'prophesied correctly' about them, verse 7, which treats the old oracle as living speech rather than a museum piece.

The command Jesus defends comes from the heart of the Law. Exodus 20:12 stands in the Ten Commandments, and Exodus 21:17 attaches the severest penalty to cursing a parent, which shows how weighty the matter was in Israel. By citing both, Jesus argues from the Law against those who claimed to guard it.

Forward from here the thread runs through the whole New Testament. Mark's parallel adds the comment that Jesus declared all foods clean, Mark 7:19. Peter, who here needs the saying explained, receives its practical meaning in the vision of Acts 10:15, and the Jerusalem council confirms that God 'cleansed their hearts by faith', Acts 15:9, so that Gentile believers carry no food or washing yoke. Paul can then say that nothing is unclean in itself, Romans 14:14, and warns against rules of 'do not handle, do not taste', Colossians 2:21 to 23. Over all of this stands the promise of Ezekiel 36:25 to 27, in which God Himself does the cleansing that no rule could.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew writes for a community of Jewish believers and Gentile hearers who have to know how to live under the Law now that its fulfiller has come. The first thing he wants them to grasp is who holds authority over God's people. Jesus does not argue that tradition is worthless; He argues that it cannot sit above Scripture. When the two collide, as with Corban, God's word wins and the human rule must give way.

The second thing is a new reading of purity. Matthew's readers would have felt the pull of the food and washing customs from both sides, from the synagogue on one hand and the surrounding world on the other. By recording that Jesus moved the question from the table to the heart, and by preserving the vice list of verse 19, he gives them a test that works in any culture: look at what comes out of a person, not at what goes in.

Finally, Matthew means this to prepare them for the mission. The next scene takes Jesus to Tyre and Sidon, and a church that will gather Gentiles needs to have heard Him say that the old boundary lines no longer decide who is clean. The warning to the disciples to leave the blind guides alone, verse 14, also tells them how to respond to leaders who will not listen: do not be swayed, and do not be intimidated.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records a dispute and a diagnosis, and it prescribes something larger than either. The washing custom is described, not commanded, and Jesus does not forbid washing hands; hygiene is a good thing, and nothing here argues against it. What He denies is that a human rule can bind the conscience as though it were God's word.

The vice list of verse 19 is also descriptive in form, naming what actually comes out of human hearts, but its force is prescriptive: these things are real defilement, and the reader is to take them seriously and bring them to God. The list follows the order of the second table of the Law, murder, adultery, theft, false testimony, so Jesus is showing that the commandments are really about the heart.

Care is needed in application. It would be a mistake to read the chapter as permission to dismiss every church custom or confession; the issue is when a custom is made equal to Scripture or used to evade it. It would be an equal mistake to read 'what enters the mouth' as a licence for gluttony or drunkenness. Those are the heart's appetites showing, and Scripture elsewhere calls them sins.

debates.question: Does Jesus here abolish the Old Testament food laws?

views.label: Yes, He sets them aside
views.case: The wording is broad: a man is not defiled by what enters his mouth, verse 11, and the explanation in verse 17 treats food as a matter of the stomach and not of the heart. Mark 7:19 adds that all foods are clean, and Acts 10:15 and Romans 14:14 read as applying the same principle. Many see this as the first move in the shift from the ceremonial law to the new covenant.

views.label: No, the dispute is about the tradition of the elders
views.case: The charge in verse 2 is about washing hands, which is not a Torah command, and Jesus has just defended the written command about parents. On this reading He is not discussing the dietary laws of Leviticus 11 at all, and the later church recognized the change only when Peter's vision came in Acts 10, which would be odd if Jesus had said it plainly here.

views.label: He relativizes them without yet abolishing them
views.case: Jesus does not cancel the laws in this scene, but He teaches a principle that makes them penultimate, and the full effect appears after the cross. Matthew 5:17 says He came to fulfill the Law, and fulfilling can mean bringing a shadow to its substance.

debates.bearing: All three agree that Jesus puts the heart above ritual and that the moral law remains. The disagreement is about timing, and the disciples' own slowness, Peter asking for an explanation in verse 15 and later needing a vision, suggests the implications took time to be seen. Believers today are free to eat anything with thanks, 1 Timothy 4:4 and 5, and must never make food a ground of fellowship.

debates.question: What is the plant that the Father has not planted?

views.label: The Pharisees and their teaching
views.case: The verse follows the Pharisees' offence, verse 12, and is followed by 'blind guides', verse 14. The image of planting and uprooting is used for God's dealings with nations and leaders in the prophets, so this reads as a warning of judgment.

views.label: The tradition itself, apart from persons
views.case: Jesus has just contrasted the precepts of men with the word of God, so the unplanted plant may be the human rules rather than the people who hold them. Individuals who are led astray could still turn and be rescued, and the verse need not close the door on them.

debates.bearing: The two overlap, since persons and teaching are bound together in this passage. What matters for the reader is that God will not let a self-made religion stand, and that the proper response is to leave it alone rather than argue it into fitness, verse 14.

study.originalLanguages:
Verses 2 and 3 are linked by a verb the English hides. The leaders ask why the disciples 'break' the tradition, and Jesus replies by asking why they 'break' the command of God. The Greek verb in both is parabaino, literally to step across or alongside, and so to transgress. Jesus hands the leaders their own word back, and it cuts the other way. The tradition of the elders is called paradosis, something handed over, a word Paul uses with approval for gospel teaching, 1 Corinthians 11:2 and 2 Thessalonians 2:15. The word itself is therefore neutral; what matters is whether what is handed down agrees with what God has said.

In verse 6 Jesus says they 'nullify' the word of God. The verb is akyroo, to make without authority, to void, the language of cancelling a legal instrument. The tradition does not merely add to the Law; it empties it of force. The same picture appears in Galatians 3:17, where Paul says a later law cannot annul a covenant already ratified.

Verse 9 is a quotation from Isaiah, but the Greek wording follows the Septuagint, which reads 'in vain', maten, where the Hebrew speaks more of fear learned by rote. Matthew's form puts the emphasis on the futility of such worship. The Hebrew says 'rules taught by men'; the Greek gives the 'commandments of men' taught as doctrines.

Verse 11 hinges on koinoo, to make common, from the adjective koinos. In Jewish usage 'common' was the opposite of holy, and to be 'defiled' was to be rendered unfit for God's presence. Jesus does not say the word is meaningless; He says its source is wrong. The verbs of motion carry the contrast, since what 'goes into' the mouth is set against what 'comes out', ekporeuomai, a verb of issuing or proceeding, used again in verse 18.

In verse 19 the heart is the source of dialogismoi poneroi, 'evil thoughts', the reasonings and schemes that precede deeds. The list that follows moves in the order of the second table of the Law: murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false testimony, slander. The last word is blasphemia, which in this context means speech that harms, and the same word is used for speech against God. In verse 13 Jesus speaks of every 'plant', phuteia, a rare picture-word in the New Testament that fits the Old Testament imagery of Israel as God's planting.

typology.type: The washing of the priests, Exodus 30:19 to 21
typology.fulfillment: The priests washed their hands and feet before they approached the altar, so that they would not die. The washing was a real act of obedience in a holy place, and the Pharisees wanted to carry it into every kitchen. The correspondence is that cleanness before God was bodily and ritual. The escalation comes in Christ, who tells His people that the cleansing they need is of the heart, and that He supplies it, Hebrews 10:22, where hearts are sprinkled clean and bodies washed. The type falls short because water reached the skin and never the conscience.

typology.type: The clean and unclean laws, Leviticus 11
typology.fulfillment: The dietary rules marked Israel as a people set apart, Leviticus 11:44 and 45. They taught that holiness touches daily life, and that some things cannot be mixed. In Christ the line is moved from the table to the heart. Peter is told 'Do not call anything impure that God has made clean', Acts 10:15, and the church is made one people from Jew and Gentile. The type falls short because it could distinguish nations but not change a heart, and so it pointed past itself to the new covenant.

typology.type: The stone heart and the heart of flesh, Ezekiel 36:25 to 27
typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel promised clean water, a new heart and a new spirit, a work only God could do. Jesus' diagnosis in verses 18 and 19 explains why the promise was needed: the trouble is inside. The fulfillment comes through Christ and His Spirit, 2 Corinthians 3:3, where the Spirit writes on hearts of flesh. The type is not so much a shadow as a promise, so it does not fall short; what remains is its full completion when believers are made new in the resurrection.

typology.type: The planting that God has not planted, verse 13
typology.fulfillment: Israel is called God's planting in Isaiah 5:7 and 61:3, and the image of uprooting speaks of judgment on whatever is not His. Jesus uses it of religious leadership that has placed human rules above God's word. The correspondence is that a vine or tree that bears no true fruit is cut off. The fulfillment comes in Christ as the true vine, John 15:1 to 5, in whom branches bear fruit. The type falls short as a picture of final fate, since the New Testament also speaks of grafting in, Romans 11:23, so that no one is beyond mercy while grace is still offered.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ first by His authority. A rabbi in that world would argue from the elders, citing earlier teachers. Jesus argues from God's word and then speaks on His own authority: 'Listen and understand', verse 10. He does not say 'it is written' of His own redefinition of purity; He simply states it, as one who is greater than the temple and Lord of the Sabbath, Matthew 12:6 and 8. When the disciples worry about the Pharisees, He speaks of 'My heavenly Father' as the planter, verse 13, claiming a relationship that no scribe could.

Second, the passage leads to Christ by diagnosis. His account of the human heart, out of which come murder, adultery and the rest, agrees with what the Old Testament says in Genesis 6:5, Genesis 8:21 and Jeremiah 17:9. If the trouble is there, then a water ritual cannot reach it, and neither can a better rule. The only remedy would be a new heart, and the prophets promised exactly that, Ezekiel 36:26. The passage therefore creates a need that it does not itself satisfy, and sends the reader forward to the cross and to the Spirit.

Third, there is a contrast of persons. The Pharisees multiply washings to be fit to eat with God; Jesus will take the unwashed, the leper, the tax collector, the Canaanite woman in the very next scene, and make them clean by His touch and word. In Matthew 8:3 He touches a leper and the leper is cleansed instead of Jesus being defiled, which reverses the direction of contagion. Holiness in Him is stronger than uncleanness. The writer of Hebrews carries the thought through: His blood cleanses the conscience from dead works, Hebrews 9:14.

A caution is needed. The passage does not say Jesus is a teacher of sincerity who would have us simply mean what we say. Its claim is sharper. The heart is the problem, and He is the cure. Readers should not make the story only a call to inner authenticity; they should let it expose the heart and send them to Him for cleansing.
study.god:
The passage shows a God who sees what people cannot hide. Isaiah's word, 'their hearts are far from Me', assumes a God who reads the heart and is not impressed by a mouth full of reverence. This agrees with 1 Samuel 16:7, where the LORD looks at the heart while man looks at appearance, and with Acts 15:8, where God is called the one who knows the heart.

He is also a God who speaks and whose speech binds. The command to honor parents is His own word, and a human tradition that cancels it has not merely erred but has set itself against Him. The doctrine of Scripture's authority is bound up here: God has spoken, and His word is not at the mercy of the community that keeps it. The same text also guards against the opposite error. A God who spoke the written command also speaks through Jesus, and so the written word is not read in isolation from the living Lord.

The chapter reveals His holiness as something deeper than ceremonial correctness. Leviticus called Israel to be holy as He is holy, Leviticus 11:44, and the Pharisees took that call seriously. Jesus does not mock the aim; He locates it. Holiness is conformity to a character, and so it begins within. This is why the word on His heavenly Father planting, verse 13, matters: what God plants bears fruit that He recognizes, and what He has not planted will not last.

There is a tension to hold. God is severe toward self-made religion, 'pulled up by its roots', and yet He is patient with confusion. The disciples, who do not understand, are not uprooted but taught, 'Do you still not understand?', verse 16. He distinguishes the hardened leader from the slow learner.

For worship, this means that no amount of liturgy can stand in for a heart turned to Him, and that no heart-religion can despise the word He gave. It means too that the believer can approach God without fear of ritual failure, since the cleanness that counts is supplied by Him, as Ezekiel promised and as the new covenant gives, Hebrews 10:22.

crossReferences.note: The oracle Jesus quotes. Isaiah describes people who draw near with their mouths and honor God with their lips while their hearts stay far away, and whose worship is rules taught by men. Jesus says the prophecy fits the leaders from Jerusalem exactly, so the problem is an old one that returns in every generation.

The fifth commandment, and the first with a promise attached. Jesus chooses it because the Corban practice reduced it to nothing while sounding devout. The command has a long reach: honor means practical support, and a vow that excuses it has set a human rule above God's word.

The penalty for cursing a parent, which Jesus quotes alongside the command to honor. By citing the severe sentence He shows how serious God considers the matter, and how serious the leaders' evasion is by comparison.

The parallel account, with extra detail for non-Jewish readers: it explains the Jewish washing customs, gives the word Corban, and adds the comment that all foods are clean. It also lengthens the vice list with greed, deceit, envy, arrogance and folly, which shows the list is illustrative and not exhaustive.

Peter's rooftop vision. The man who asked Jesus to explain the saying in verse 15 is told three times not to call anything impure that God has made clean. It shows the principle Jesus taught became practice only when God moved, and that apostles needed time to catch up.

The diagnosis that stands behind verse 19. The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure, and the next verses answer that God searches the heart. Jesus' teaching is not a new anthropology but a reminder of what the prophets already said.

The promise that answers the problem. God will sprinkle clean water, cleanse from impurities and idols, remove the heart of stone and give a heart of flesh, and put His Spirit within. Where the leaders offered external washing, God promises a washing that changes the person from within.

The same charge, later and fuller. Jesus says the scribes and Pharisees clean the outside of the cup and dish while the inside is full of greed and self-indulgence, and tells them to clean the inside first. Together with this passage it forms a pair that exposes the failure of outward religion.

An earlier statement of the same principle: out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks. It supports verse 18, that what comes out of the mouth comes from the heart, and shows that the teaching on defilement is consistent with how Matthew presents Jesus' view of speech.

David's prayer after his sin: create in me a clean heart. It shows that a godly Israelite already understood that cleansing is God's creative work and cannot be achieved by washing. The prayer is an Old Testament answer to the Pharisees' question about what makes a person fit for God.

Paul takes up the same issue for a new setting. Rules like 'Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch' have an appearance of wisdom but are of no value against the indulgence of the flesh. They rest on human commands, which is Jesus' own judgment on the tradition of the elders.

Peter's report to the council. God made no distinction between Jew and Gentile, for He cleansed their hearts by faith. This is the settled conclusion of what Jesus began here: the cleansing that counts is of the heart, and it comes through faith and the gift of the Spirit.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture begins with a good world and a pair who had nothing to hide. After the fall the problem is no longer something outside them but a bent within, which Genesis 6:5 and 8:21 state flatly. This passage takes that old diagnosis and sets it beside the long attempt of Israel's religion to manage defilement by washings, offerings and rules. Those provisions were God's gift, a school for a people who needed to learn that He is holy and they are not. Jesus does not discard the school; He announces that its graduation day has come and that the thing it taught about, a cleansed heart, is now to be given.

Looking back, the chapter answers a question left open since Eden: how can unclean people live with a holy God? The Law's answer was distance and ritual repair. The prophets' answer was a promise, in Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:26, that God would change the heart and give His Spirit. Jesus here shows that the promise is needed because the heart is the source of the trouble, and then in the same Gospel He will pay for it, in Matthew 26:28, where His blood is poured out for the forgiveness of sins.

Looking forward, this scene opens the door to the nations. A church that no longer sorts people by food or ritual can receive Gentiles on the basis of faith alone, which is what Peter learns in Acts 10 and what the council confirms in Acts 15. The very next episode of Matthew shows it happening, when Jesus enters the region of Tyre and Sidon.

In the new creation, the clean heart becomes the whole person. The pure in heart will see God, Matthew 5:8, and nothing impure will enter the city, Revelation 21:27. What the Pharisees sought with washing, and could not reach, God completes in His people. The distinctions of clean and unclean fall away not because holiness has been lowered but because it has been given, so that the people who walk with Him are made fit to do so.

quiz.q: What was the real problem with the Pharisees' tradition of hand washing?

options.text: They elevated human tradition above God's command, even using it to sidestep His word.
options.note: Verses 3-6 show tradition being used to nullify the command to honor parents.

options.text: They added extra rules that were not in the Law of Moses.
options.note: True, the washing was a human addition, but the deeper fault was setting tradition against God's own command.

options.text: They were too concerned about physical cleanliness and hygiene.
options.note: The issue is not hygiene at all but authority and the heart; this misplaces the emphasis.

options.text: They failed to wash their hands often enough themselves.
options.note: Jesus is not endorsing the washing rule; the charge is against the tradition, not their neglect of it.

quiz.q: According to Jesus, what truly defiles a person?

options.text: The evil that comes out of the heart, such as evil thoughts, malice, and deceit.
options.note: Verses 18-19 trace defilement to the heart within.

options.text: The sinful words and actions a person produces.
options.note: True, these defile, but Jesus traces them back to their source, the heart, which this answer omits.

options.text: Certain unclean foods that enter the mouth.
options.note: Jesus explicitly denies this; what enters the mouth does not defile the person.

options.text: Contact with ceremonially unclean people or objects.
options.note: Jesus relocates defilement from external contact to the inner heart.

quiz.q: How does Jesus describe the worship of the leaders, quoting Isaiah?

options.text: They honor God with their lips while their hearts are far from Him.
options.note: Verses 8-9 quote Isaiah 29:13 on hollow, hypocritical worship.

options.text: They worship sincerely but follow the wrong traditions.
options.note: Partly right about the traditions, but Jesus calls the worship itself vain and the heart distant, not sincere.

options.text: They worship God correctly but lack enough zeal.
options.note: The problem is not too little zeal but a heart far from God behind the outward show.

options.text: They no longer perform any worship at all.
options.note: They worship diligently, but in vain; the issue is the heart, not the absence of worship.

quiz.q: What does this passage reveal about the kind of cleansing people need?

options.text: A cleansing of the heart, which no external ritual can accomplish.
options.note: Since defilement rises from the heart, cleansing must reach that deep, pointing to the new covenant work of Christ.

options.text: A more careful keeping of the outward purity laws.
options.note: This gets the seriousness of purity but looks in the wrong place; the heart, not the outside, is the issue.

options.text: A cleansing that comes simply by human effort and self-discipline.
options.note: The heart's corruption runs too deep for self-reform; it needs the renewing work Jesus brings.

options.text: No cleansing at all, since the heart cannot be changed.
options.note: Scripture promises a new heart; Jesus comes precisely to cleanse and renew it.

questions: Jesus warned against letting tradition override God's word. Where might a comfortable custom or assumption be quietly displacing what Scripture actually says in your life?
The leaders honored God with their lips while their hearts were far from Him. What would it look like for your worship this week to close that gap between words and heart?
Jesus traced sin to the heart, not the hands. When you are tempted to manage sin by managing appearances, how does His diagnosis change the way you pray?
The Corban loophole let people look devout while neglecting their parents. Is there a place where religious language is masking a duty of love you are avoiding?
Only a new heart can make the unclean clean. How does knowing that Jesus cleanses from the inside out free you from mere outward striving?

translationNotes.note: Jesus cites Exodus 20:12 and Deuteronomy 5:16 (honor your father and mother) together with Exodus 21:17 and Leviticus 20:9; the two quotations are joined here with the word and for a clean reading.
The gift devoted to God reflects the Corban vow; some manuscripts read his father or mother, others his father only. The sense is unchanged: the vow was used to withhold support owed to parents.
